Itinérance: survivre à une nuit glaciale: Homelessness: Surviving a Freezing Night in Downtown Montréal
Mardi soir, une nuit polaire à Montréal,: On Tuesday night, a polar night in Montréal, École Converse documents the efforts of people experiencing homelessness to keep warm.
Des personnes en situation d'itinérance: People experiencing homelessness outside the Mission Old Brewery. Photo: Amélie Rock
Salut, c’est Loubna avec Aya, Firas, Aud: Hi, it’s Loubna with Aya, Firas, Aude, Cindy, Sènan and Chris!
Je vous propose aujourd’hui un article u: Today I’m bringing you a slightly special article, because it was produced by five École Converse students with the support of Christopher Curtis, co-founder of the independent media outlet The Rover; Lela Savic, editor-in-chief of La Converse; and myself.
Après plusieurs semaines de formation, A: After several weeks of training, Aya, Firas, Aude, Cindy and Sènan went out into the field to better understand the challenge people experiencing homelessness face in surviving a freezing night in downtown Montréal. The subject imposed itself with the arrival of an intense cold snap in recent days.
Christopher Curtis leur a donné quelques: Christopher Curtis gave them some advice on how to do good fieldwork reporting, dare to approach people in vulnerable situations and learn to observe details.
Je suis particulièrement fière de ce rep: I’m particularly proud of this report, which is the very first article for some of these budding journalists. I want to stress that the result lives up to their talent! Thank you to Chris for his journalistic generosity, and thank you to Aude, Cindy, Sènan, Firas and Aya for their commitment.
<strong>Alors qu’une nouvelle vague de f: As a new cold snap hits Montréal, the risk of people experiencing homelessness losing their lives while spending the night outside is high. On Tuesday evening, a public consultation was held on homelessness and the issue of social cohabitation. Outside, the only question was survival. A report by École Converse.
19 h. La séance « Itinérance et cohabita: 7 p.m. The “Homelessness and Social Cohabitation” session, organized by the Office de consultation publique de Montréal (OCPM), begins at the Centre Saint-Pierre. The goal is to gather the public’s views on an issue that has generated a great deal of debate: homelessness.
La métropole concentrait en effet 47 % d: Indeed, the metropolis accounted for 47% of the people experiencing homelessness counted in Quebec in 2022, or 4,690 people. According to several community organizations, that figure is largely underestimated and does not reflect hidden homelessness, which refers to people staying with friends or sleeping in their cars.
Sur l’estrade, six personnes viennent pr: On the stage, six people are presenting this information session, the first in a public consultation process that will run until February 28. They are three OCPM commissioners, two representatives of the City of Montréal’s Service de la diversité et de l’inclusion sociale (SDIS) and an adviser from the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM).
Au fond de la salle, les retardataires s: At the back of the room, latecomers help themselves to a cup of coffee, offered free to the public. While outside, people without shelter pile on layers of clothing to dull the bite of the cold, in here people take off their coats as soon as they walk in because it’s so warm.
« Les ressources consacrées aux personne: “The resources devoted to people experiencing homelessness are truly essential to reducing homelessness, but also to meeting the basic needs of vulnerable people and promoting their inclusion. Perhaps most people agree that the services are necessary, but it’s often the location of those services that is hard to reach consensus on,” says Nicolas Pagot, division head at the City of Montréal’s Service de la diversité et de l’inclusion sociale (SDIS).
Les cas de mobilisation du voisinage lor: Cases of neighbours mobilizing against announced projects for homeless shelters, for example, are indeed commonplace. The City nevertheless says it wants to “set up resources in all 19 boroughs” so that they are no longer concentrated downtown.
Les bancs réservés au public sont clairs: The benches reserved for the public are sparsely filled: about fifteen citizens answered the invitation, while 50 people follow the proceedings online. Some addressed the representatives. “You said you want resources in every borough, but also that it’s hard to reach a consensus; so can you give us an idea of when you hope to achieve this goal?” a woman asks at the microphone.
Certains citoyens ont posé des questions: Some citizens asked questions during the “Homelessness and Social Cohabitation” public consultation held at the Centre Saint-Pierre on Tuesday evening. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Les réponses ne sont pas toujours au ren: The answers aren’t always forthcoming… In this case, as on several occasions, the City’s representatives dodge the question. “And that’s it? You have no answer to give?” the chair of the consultation, Ariane Émond, asks them. As laughter ripples through the room, the City’s representatives promise a written answer at a later date.
Elle s’interroge sur le bien-fondé des r: She questions the soundness of the regulations and safety standards that keep vacant buildings, of which there are many in Montréal, from being used to shelter people experiencing homelessness, especially during extreme cold episodes. She is looking here for answers to her questions: “I understand that there are standards in general, but in this specific case, I don’t understand how it would be more dangerous for homeless people to sleep in heated buildings, even if they aren’t up to code, than to sleep outside and risk freezing to death.”
Là encore, Nicolas Pagot contourne la qu: Once again, Nicolas Pagot sidesteps the question: he merely reminds the audience that “identifying a space for a resource involves a lot of criteria,” notably “in terms of fire safety.”
À l’extérieur, tout près de cette salle: Outside, steps away from this enveloping, warm room where people are discussing the fact that their presence must be socially acceptable, those most affected don’t have the luxury of pirouetting their way out of the cold. Their only concern that night, which they know will be particularly icy, is to survive.
<strong>21 h – Une nuit au chaud, une mi: 9 p.m. – A warm night, a daily mission
À quelques mètres seulement du faste du: Just a few metres from the splendour of the Montréal courthouse, a completely different world unfolds in the shadows, gripping the snowy ground. Here, there is no marble or gilding, only duffel bags and hard lives. A dignity slung over the shoulder under the frost.
Il est 21 h et, dans la pénombre d’une p: It is 9 p.m. and, in the dimness of a building doorway, under the clouds of smoke from their cigarettes, John and Denis are getting ready to spend a long night outside. Perhaps the coldest of the year.
Les minutes s’égrènent lentement, alors: The minutes tick slowly by as they talk about the roofs that might shelter them tonight. It doesn’t matter: an ATM vestibule, the entrance of a closed shop, any place where the cold would be a little less biting… “You’re lucky, you’ve got a bed for tonight,” Denis says to his companion in misfortune. John was able to find respite at the shelter tonight.
Denis, la soixantaine et la barbe grison: Denis, in his sixties with a graying beard, opens up: “At some point, you’re so wiped out that you fall asleep, even with the lights on.” Another, younger man adds: “Outside, it’s impossible to sleep more than 10 minutes in a row. It’s so cold that you wake up constantly.” When asked whether they have received any help or support from outside their community, Denis answers: “Not really. But among ourselves, yes.”
Un peu plus loin, devant le refuge de la: A little further on, outside the shelter on Clark Street, a strange normalcy sets in. Some greet each other, exchange smiles, know one another. It almost looks like a summer terrace, but the words echo in the frozen air, and hands clutch blankets. The little they have, they share: a cigarette, a coffee, a moment of humanity.
Pourtant, derrière la vitre du Café Miss: And yet, behind the window of the Café Mission, there is warmth. The evening crowd, large at the shelter, watched the Canadiens beat the Lightning late in the game on TV. A small break in the clouds on many faces marked by weariness and a feeling of abandonment.
Derrière le Café Mission, dans une ruell: Behind the Café Mission, in a dark alley, we run into George Hadland. Originally from New Brunswick, he has lived in Montréal for 20 years. With a sincere smile and natural warmth, this resident of the neighbourhood opens the trunk of his car.
Derrière le Café Mission, George Hadland: Behind the Café Mission, George Hadland brings supplies for people experiencing homelessness. Photo: Amélie Rock
À l’intérieur, des couvertures, des chau: Inside are blankets, shoes, hot and cold drinks. George, who is always ready to lend a hand, invites us to warm up. “Do you want something? A beer? A blanket?” We’ll pass on the beer tonight, but his kindness is already warming hearts.
« C’est dur de les voir dans ce froid, c: “It’s hard to see them in this cold,” he confides. “But if we can do something, even something small, it counts. I buy blankets, coats, things like that. I like doing this and going around my neighbourhood. It’s important to show that we care about others.”
George ne baisse pas les bras. « Ça fait: George isn’t giving up. “I’ve been doing this for four or five years,” he says. “Before, it was less bad, but now there are a lot more people. Everyone deserves a roof, and that’s what motivates me. I tell myself: ‘Today it’s particularly cold, we have to go.’ Yesterday I was stuck with my wife and the kids, but today, we’re here. We collect stuff, blankets, hats, everything we can to help.”
Tandis que l’arche du Quartier chinois c: While the arch of Chinatown celebrates the memory of its pioneers, several homeless people struggle to survive at its feet. Some will spend the night outside for lack of a place in a shelter. They too hope for a thought, an open door. Yet year after year, their distress grows.
<strong>21 h 56 – Des rues désertées par: 9:56 p.m. – Deserted streets at -15°C under the Jacques-Cartier Bridge
À l’intersection des avenues De Lorimier: At the intersection of De Lorimier Avenue and Viger Avenue East, under the imposing metal structure of the Jacques-Cartier Bridge, calm reigns. In the pale light of the streetlamps, shadows stretch across a frozen scene.
Un abri de fortune est dressé là, sur la: A makeshift shelter stands there, on the snow, made of plastic tarps held in place by pieces of wood clumsily arranged. Right beside it, an image of impossible movement, an abandoned bicycle, its front wheel missing, lies sadly. Around the tent, scattered pieces of a life. A powder-pink scarf lies in the soiled snow, next to worn mittens, a reminder of a recent presence.
Au sol, des restes de bois calciné témoi: On the ground, the remains of charred wood bear witness to a feeble attempt to fend off the cold. A small flame, probably lit by rudimentary means, must have offered brief relief to one or more people. But tonight, the scene is empty. No breath, no voice, just the distant murmur of traffic on the bridge.
Une tente abandonnée en dessous du pont: An abandoned tent under the Jacques-Cartier Bridge. Photo: Amélie Rock
À nos appels pour savoir si quelqu’un se: When we call out to ask whether anyone is in the tent, no one answers. The contrast is striking. Here, under this bridge in a city bustling with activity, abandonment is palpable.
Où sont-ils partis ? Ont-ils trouvé refu: Where did they go? Did they find shelter elsewhere, or are they still wandering in search of a less inhospitable place? These questions remain unanswered, just like the cold that creeps in everywhere.
<strong>22 h 38 – La joie de trouver un: 10:38 p.m. – The joy of finding a coat
Alors que nous marchons vers Atwater, à: As we walk toward Atwater, at the corner of Saint-Hubert Street and Viger Avenue, the silhouette of a man standing alone at the red light catches our attention. He calls out to us. His gaze is gentle, but tired. We offer him something to eat, and his face lights up at once. Gratefully, he talks with us for a moment and briefly tells us about his daily life.
« Si vous voulez, allez vers Concordia,: “If you want, go toward Concordia, next to the A&W,” he recommends. “My friends are there. They’ll be very happy, because yesterday they were really hungry and couldn’t find anything to eat.” We sense an unshakeable kindness and solidarity.
La plupart du temps, il essaie de trouve: Most of the time, he tries to find a place to sleep, but it’s not always easy. Sometimes, when he falls asleep on the street, people go through his pockets, taking what he has that is most precious: often a few coins or small objects…
Mais ce mardi soir, il est soulagé. « Je: But this Tuesday night, he is relieved. “I’m sleeping at someone’s place, on the floor, but it’s warm,” he says with a shy smile. Then, as if to share a little joy, he proudly shows us his coat. “Look! I found it on the street. You see it? It’s nice, right?” His eyes shine as he strokes the fabric, happy with his find.
<strong>23 h 01 – McDonald’s au coin Atw: 11:01 p.m. – McDonald’s at the corner of Atwater and Sainte-Catherine: 30 minutes and then out
À deux pas du square Cabot, entre l’odeu: A stone’s throw from Cabot Square, between the smell of fried food and that of cleaning products, we walk past the glowing M and into the famous fast-food chain, one of the places where homeless people take refuge to find a little warmth. Several try to bargain for a few hours of respite inside the McDonald’s, but are chased out. Outside, the cold is biting, at -15°C.
Quelques minutes plus tard, un employé –: A few minutes later, an employee, whom we’ll call Paul to protect his anonymity, starts his shift. First task of the evening? Kicking out the two homeless people asleep in the dining room. He pulls on latex gloves and gets ready to wake the first of them.
Celle-ci est assise sur la banquette et: She is sitting on the bench seat, curled up, her head between her arms on the table. She is wearing a coat and sunglasses and lifts her head only for a few seconds when knocks echo on the table. Just afterward, she is approached by Ethan, a man experiencing homelessness who seems to know the sleeping woman. He talks to her and tries in turn to wake her. He pulls her arm, takes her pulse to make sure she is okay and shakes her so that she gets up and leaves with him.
« C’est très difficile. C’est sûr que, s: “It’s very hard. Of course, if I had the choice, I’d do another job,” says Paul. Having recently arrived in Canada, he knew when he took the position that he would have to interact frequently with people experiencing homelessness. “But I didn’t expect at all to see this in Canada. It’s very shocking to see so many people using drugs in public spaces and so many people sleeping outside in this cold,” he says.
Nous sommes là depuis 20 minutes quand u: We have been there for 20 minutes when a woman walks into the building. She lets out a sigh of despair on learning that the washroom is now inaccessible, locked and gated. “It’s closed at night because we were finding too many used injection supplies in the washrooms. We reopen in the morning, but often with someone monitoring,” confirms an employee.
« Ça ne me dérange pas s’ils mangent ou: “I don’t mind if they eat or if they sit down to have something. Management gives them 30 minutes to warm up, but the agreement is that they leave afterward to make room for customers. Sometimes I even give them food for free, but the problem is the ones who show up high and vandalize and steal,” explains Paul, pointing to a television that was damaged six months ago. On the walls and pillars of the restaurant, there are indeed signs from management with a clear message: the dining room is only open to customers who are buying something, for a maximum of 30 minutes.
Les personnes en situation d'itinérance: People experiencing homelessness can warm up for 30 minutes at the McDonald’s at Alexis Nihon. Photo: Amélie Rock
Plus préoccupant, Paul a déjà été agress: More worrying, Paul has been assaulted several times. “Last week, a man pulled out a knife; it happens sometimes. I’m not afraid, I know how to handle them, but it’s not easy,” he sighs before heading toward another person lying on the floor.
Cachée sous son manteau, celle-ci sommei: Hidden under a coat, this person is dozing. After several attempts, they still can’t stand up. Three police officers come into the restaurant and head for the counter, but the employee calls out to them and asks for their help. They too are unable to get the person to stand, and the person ends up leaving the restaurant in an ambulance.
Les agents du SPVM sont habitués à ce ge: SPVM officers are used to this kind of scene downtown. “Sometimes there are people sleeping in alleys or on buses, and we’ll wake them up because we wonder if they’re still alive,” says one of them.
« En hiver, c’est pratiquement ça, notre: “In winter, that’s practically our job: looking for people experiencing homelessness to make sure they’re not in danger and trying to find them somewhere to go. When we find someone, we call the shelters to see if there’s room. If there is, we accompany them, but sometimes the shelters are full, and there’s nothing else we can do,” the officer continues. These are situations that don’t leave him indifferent and in response to which he has learned to develop a certain kind of “resilience” in order to continue his mission of “protecting the most vulnerable.”
<strong>23 h 34 – Rejetés, ils errent da: 11:34 p.m. – Turned away, they wander in the cold in search of a new refuge
De l’autre côté de l’avenue Atwater, le: Across Atwater Avenue, the rule is the same at the A&W. The welcome is hardly easier: people experiencing homelessness can’t stay more than a few minutes. The atmosphere grows heavier, time is running out: they have to find a place to rest.
« J’ai l’impression de ne pas avoir dorm: “I feel like I haven’t slept in years,” repeats the woman who found the washroom closed at McDonald’s, over and over. She worries as winters grow ever icier.
Lorsqu’elle n’a pas le choix, elle se ré: When she has no choice, she takes refuge at the hospital. However, she tries to avoid that place, where, among other things, it is impossible to smoke.
Alors qu’elle nous confie ses inquiétude: As she shares her worries with us, Ethan, a man with an exhausted gaze, finally comes out of the restaurant, expelled by police officers and an employee. Cigarette between his lips, he walks away with a friend, looking for the next place of respite. Several spots and shelters are full, and they list the few options they have left.
Pendant qu’ils finissent leurs cigarette: While they finish their cigarettes, we tell them about a warming centre on Stanley Street, about a 20-minute walk away. Ethan and his friend admit, with a hint of surprise, that they didn’t know it existed. The police never tell them where these shelters are, forcing them to walk aimlessly in the cold.
Ce centre de réchauffement présente tout: This warming centre has one major drawback, however: they can’t sleep there. The place offers only temporary relief. Ethan and his friend walk off, setting out toward the warming centre, their silhouettes gradually melting into the darkness.
Sophia, deux chapeaux vissés sur la tête: Sophia, two hats pulled down over her head and eyes full of gentleness, has listened to the whole conversation. Silent until now, she speaks up… She has been in Montréal for almost a year. She is originally from Kangiqsujuaq, a small village in Nunavik. Located near Hudson Strait and Baffin Island, it has barely 840 residents sharing their daily lives there.
En raison de la crise du logement, sa fa: Because of the housing crisis, her family had to move to Nova Scotia. She does have a few cousins in the city, but a void remains. The absence of her loved ones and her former life is keenly felt.
« Il fait vraiment froid », s’exclame-t-: “It’s really cold,” she exclaims, teeth clenched and lips trembling. She glances at her phone, waiting for news from her cousin.
« Dieu m’a donné cette vie », souffle-t-: “God gave me this life,” she whispers. Despite her hardships, she does everything she can to help others, particularly young Inuit women living on the streets of Montréal. “It’s easy to end up in the wrong circles,” says Sophia. She often reads judgment in the eyes of passersby, a look that weighs heavily. So she tries as much as she can to create a space where these young women are supported and valued.
Avant de poursuivre son chemin, elle nou: Before continuing on her way, she reassures us all the same: she has a place to sleep.
À une rue de là, on trouve l’espace urba: A block away is the Cabot Square urban space. A tent named in honour of Raphaël Napa André used to be set up there. The Innu man died in January 2021 on the streets of Montréal. On a freezing night, he was forced to leave a shelter because of COVID-19 restrictions.
La population en situation d’itinérance: People experiencing homelessness in Cabot Square and the surrounding area used to gather there, where a number of services were offered. Hot drinks, seats to warm up in, blankets and coats to stay warm, as well as food and feminine hygiene products were available to anyone who needed them.
Mais depuis deux ans, la Ville a cessé d: But for the past two years, the City has stopped putting up the tent. A skating rink has been installed in its place. Condos and luxury apartments have replaced the gas station, and the old Montreal Children’s Hospital has been relocated. The Atwater metro station adds to this burden, its doors now closed and locked, impossible to brave to escape the cold.
<strong>Pas de mort à déplorer ce soir-l: No deaths to mourn that night… but tomorrow?
Personne n’est mort ou n’a été conduit a: No one died or was taken to the emergency room for frostbite.
Le succès dans les rues de Montréal se m: Success on Montréal’s streets is thus measured less by what was accomplished than by what was avoided. As Tuesday night gave way to Wednesday, and an Arctic cold settled over the city’s 5,000 homeless people, death lurked on every street corner.
Si on ne fait rien, le froid enveloppe l: If nothing is done, the cold closes in on the vital organs. It slows the heart, fills the lungs with fluid and numbs the part of the brain that regulates body temperature.
Au lever du jour, devant Résilience Mont: At daybreak, outside Résilience Montréal, escaping that fate feels less like a victory than a reprieve. That is what David Chapman, manager of the downtown shelter, told La Converse early Wednesday morning.
« Parfois, on a l’impression de jouer av: “Sometimes it feels like we’re gambling with their lives and not losing,” he says. “But there are plenty of cold nights still ahead, and it’s almost certain we’ll lose more people before spring arrives.”
Si la chance a permis à de nombreux sans: While luck allowed many homeless people to survive, there was also a good deal of preparation on the part of Montréal’s emergency services. Patrol officers “checked and rechecked” every corner of their sector, according to police spokesperson Jean-Pierre Brabant.
« Nous effectuons des rondes dans les ca: “We’re doing rounds of the encampments and the alleys, everyone is mobilized,” Brabant told us. “On a night like that, if someone needs to be transported or is in distress, our mission is to help them.”
De même, les ambulanciers de la ville on: Likewise, the city’s paramedics kept an eye out for anyone at risk of frostbite.
« Nos premiers répondants sont tous parf: “Our first responders are all fully aware of the danger outside right now,” adds a spokesperson for Urgences-santé.
M. Chapman surveille ces coins de rue de: Chapman has been watching over these street corners for about a decade. When he started, this shelter in the west end of downtown took in 100 to 150 people. Today, the number is more than 300.
Avant la pandémie, quelques cérémonies c: Before the pandemic, a few memorial ceremonies were held each year in memory of people who had died on the street. The shelter would hang their photos on a wall and hold a funeral service.
Mais au cours des cinq dernières années,: But over the past five years, the situation has deteriorated to the point that deaths are now commemorated in group ceremonies. Last summer, the shelter honoured the memory of 37 people during an afternoon at Cabot Square. They had died within a span of 18 months.
« Avant, nous perdions trois ou quatre p: “We used to lose three or four people a year,” Chapman explains. “It was hard, but we didn’t know back then how much worse it would get. Now, sometimes there are three deaths in a month.”
Avec l’augmentation fulgurante du prix d: With the skyrocketing cost of housing in Montréal since 2020, the streets and shelters are overflowing. And with the Tribunal administratif du logement (TAL)’s recent recommendation to raise rents by 6% this year, it looks like the streets will become even more crowded.
« Personne ne veut traverser la ville à: “Nobody wants to walk across the city only to be turned away from a shelter because it’s full,” Chapman points out. “Right now, in some places, you have a fifty-fifty chance of being turned away. We can’t keep relying on chance like this without paying the price.”
Dans le public, on trouve notamment Hélo: Among those in the audience is Héloïse Koltuk, who works at Entremise, a Montréal company that creates living spaces in vacant buildings. “Every day I see people sleeping at my door, outside in the cold, while I manage a huge, heated, empty building,” the young professional explains. M<sup>s</sup> Koltuk looks after a building a stone’s throw from Berri-UQAM station, right near the Gare d’autocars de Montréal and the BAnQ, an area she describes as “the showcase of homelessness in Montréal.”
